summary: Light at the north side of the Minas Basin entrance by Parrsboro, lit 1886; the Coast Guard still lists an occulting light, but sources disagree on which tower stands today.

structures.note: First tower, 34 ft per Lighthouse Friends; the Society and a tourism guide describe a tapered square wooden tower as still standing

Lighthouse Friends dates the present pepper-shaker-style tower to 1973; the Coast Guard list gives a white square tower with red upper portion, 11.7 m. Which tower stands is not settled by the sources read.

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property. Road too rutted and overgrown to drive; about 1.3 km walk. Grounds open, tower closed.

events.note: Placed in service 1 November 1886 with a square white wooden tower and attached dwelling
Hand fog horn given to keeper Elisha Phinney
Fog alarm building in rectangular wooden form put in operation 1 March 1904; built by A. H. Dyer of Parrsboro for $1,307
3-inch diaphone installed in place of the earlier diaphone to increase the power of the fog alarm
Fixed red light changed to occulting white, 7 s on and 3 s eclipse, with fourth-order dioptric apparatus (report labelled 1911)
Society dates fourth-order dioptric lens to 1922-1941; the 1911 report already describes fourth-order dioptric apparatus
Oil storage tank installed at the light (report labelled 1922)
Diaphone fog signal in a separate building (Society)
Present tower and keeper's dwelling, per Lighthouse Friends. The Society and a tourism guide describe the 1886 tower as still standing.
Destaffed in 1988 (Lighthouse Friends); the Society gives 'automated by 1989'
Electric light, fourth-order dioptric lens and electric fog horn (Society)

notes_for_editor: Low confidence because the sources disagree on the present tower and the fourth-order lens. (1) Which tower stands: Lighthouse Friends says the present pepper-shaker-style tower dates from 1973; the Society's record (tapered square wood tower, still standing) and a tourism guide both describe the 1886 wooden tower with its attached dwelling as still standing; the Coast Guard list gives a white square tower with a red upper portion, 11.7 m high. The station record's wood material and 11.7 m height come from the Coast Guard list and Wikidata, not from a dated description of the present tower. A human should check a photo or a Coast Guard inspection before the page says which tower stands. (2) Fourth-order lens year: the Society gives 1922-1941; the Marine report labelled 1911 already describes a fourth-order dioptric light at Cape Sharp. Not resolved; the story gives both. (3) Operating status: the Society's index says 'Still Operating: No'; the Coast Guard list gives 'Operates 24 h.' The story gives both. The Society's record may be stale; not verified. (4) Keeper table (Marine report labelled 1911, scan p. 242, printed p. 235) was checked on the page image on 2026-10-28: the row reads Cape Sharpe, Freeman Yorke, appointed June 30 1902, so the pairing is confirmed and matches the Lighthouse Friends roster. (5) Gap: no keeper is listed in any source read between Durrant (to 1954) and Green (from 1963). (6) The Georges are listed as separate keepers; no source says they were related, and none is inferred. The Marine report labelled 1923 names a 'Mr. J. E. George' making spar buoys at Cape Sharpe; the story says the report does not call him the keeper. (7) No wreck or storm at the station is recorded in any source read. The Society's Facebook post and a Flickr caption appeared in search results only and were not read. (8) Newspapers not searched (Canadian station; Chronicling America is US). (9) Corrections: none proposed for the record. The first_lit (1886), the position and the Coast Guard characteristic agree with the list. The record's 1973 'built' event comes from Rowlett's directory, which the story cites only through Lighthouse Friends. (10) Access: the grounds are open and the tower closed; the story says so in Today. (11) Dwelling: Lighthouse Friends names the buyer; the story does not, because it is a private residence.
